title: Your setup and first Git commits
goal: Set up your tools and push your first three commits to GitHub from the terminal.

concepts: What a terminal is: cd, ls (dir on Windows), mkdir, pwd
What Git is: a history of snapshots of your project
Repository, working folder, staging area, commit
git init, git status, git add, git commit, git log
What GitHub is and how git push sends commits to it

build.task: Install VS Code and Git, create a GitHub account, and create a public repo called jobready-journey. Inside it make a folder day01 with a file about-me.md describing who you are and why you are learning. Make at least 3 separate commits from the terminal, then push.

acceptance: Repo jobready-journey is public on GitHub
At least 3 commits, each with a message that says what changed (not "update" or "final")
All commits made with git commit in the terminal, not by uploading files on the website
day01/about-me.md has all three sections filled in your own words
Root README.md says what this repo is for

hints: Work in this order: mkdir jobready-journey → cd into it → git init → create files → git status to see what Git notices.
One commit = git add <file> then git commit -m "message". Make a commit after creating README.md, another after adding about-me.md, another after filling its sections.
Create an empty repo on GitHub (no README), then run: git remote add origin https://github.com/<you>/jobready-journey.git, git branch -M main, git push -u origin main.
proof: Link to your third commit on GitHub (open the commit on github.com and copy the URL from the address bar).

explainBack.q: Using one of your own commits as the example, explain the difference between git add and git commit.
lookFor: add moves changes to the staging area
commit saves a snapshot of staged changes with a message
refers to a specific file or commit of theirs

explainBack.q: Pick one of your commit messages. What does it tell someone reading your history later, and why did you word it that way?
lookFor: message describes what changed
useful for future reader or themselves
quotes their real message

explainBack.q: Before you ran git push, where did your commits exist? What did git push change?
lookFor: commits were only in the local repository on their computer
push uploads commits to the remote (GitHub)
origin is the name of the remote

lastHintExplanation: git add chooses which changes go into the next snapshot (the staging area). git commit saves that snapshot with a message into your local history. Until you push, all of this lives only in the .git folder on your computer; git push copies your new commits to the remote called origin, which is your GitHub repo.

title: HTML page structure and text
goal: Write a valid HTML page from scratch with a correct head, heading order and text elements.

concepts: What HTML is: content described by elements and attributes
<!DOCTYPE html>, <html lang>, <head>, <body>
<meta charset> and <meta name="viewport">, <title>
Headings h1–h6 as an outline, not for font size
p, strong vs b, em vs i, blockquote, br vs new paragraph
Checking your page with the W3C validator

build.task: In day02/index.html, write an "About me" page from an empty file (no templates, no Emmet shortcuts). It needs a full head, one h1, at least two h2 sections each with an h3 inside, paragraphs, at least one strong and one em used for meaning, and a blockquote with a quote you like.

starterFiles.name: day02/index.html
starterFiles.content: <!-- Start from an empty file. Type every line yourself. -->

acceptance: Starts with <!DOCTYPE html> and has <html lang="en"> (or your language)
Head has meta charset, meta viewport and a title
Exactly one h1; h2 and h3 used in order (no skipping from h1 to h3)
strong and em each used where the meaning needs emphasis, not for looks
W3C validator shows 0 errors (paste a note in the commit message saying so)

hints: Write the skeleton first: doctype, html, head, body. Open it in the browser before adding content.
Think of headings as a book outline: h1 = book title, h2 = chapters, h3 = sections inside a chapter.
<meta charset="utf-8"> and <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"> go inside <head>. Paste your full file into validator.w3.org and fix each error from the top.
proof: Commit containing day02/index.html. Mention "validator: 0 errors" in the commit message.

explainBack.q: In your page, what would break or change if you removed the meta charset line? And the viewport line?
lookFor: charset tells browser the text encoding so characters like ₹ or Hindi display correctly
viewport makes the page size correctly on mobile instead of zoomed-out desktop width

explainBack.q: Why did you choose h2 for your sections and not h1 or h4? Point to your actual headings.
lookFor: headings form a document outline/hierarchy
one h1 for the page topic
screen readers and search engines use heading order
names their real headings

explainBack.q: Where did you use strong and em in your page, and why those instead of b and i?
lookFor: strong = strong importance, em = stress emphasis
b and i are only visual
meaning matters for screen readers
cites their real sentence

lastHintExplanation: HTML describes meaning, CSS handles looks. meta charset sets the text encoding; the viewport meta lets mobile browsers use the device width. Headings form an outline that screen readers and search engines navigate, so their order matters more than their size. strong and em carry meaning (importance, stress); b and i are only visual.

An error because of extra spaces
predict.why:
HTML collapses runs of whitespace (spaces and newlines) into a single space. Use separate

elements or CSS for layout.

The second becomes an h2 automatically

title: Links, images, lists and semantic layout
goal: Build a two-page mini site linked together, using semantic layout elements instead of plain divs.

concepts: <a href> with relative paths (projects.html, ../day02/index.html) and absolute URLs
Opening external links safely: target="_blank" with rel="noopener"
: why alt text matters
ul, ol, li and nesting lists
Semantic layout: header, nav, main, section, article, footer
Why semantic elements beat div for accessibility and SEO

build.task: In day03/, build index.html (home) and projects.html. Both pages share the same header with a nav linking to each other. Home has your photo or any image with real alt text and an ordered list of your top 3 goals. Projects has one article per planned project (at least 2) with a nested unordered list of the tech it will use, and a link to your Day 2 page.

starterFiles.name: day03/images/README.txt
starterFiles.content: Put your image here, for example me.jpg. Keep it under 300 KB.

acceptance: Both pages use header, nav, main and footer; no layout made of plain divs
Nav links work in both directions using relative paths
Image has meaningful alt text (not "image" or "photo") and width/height set
An ol on home and a nested ul inside each project article
A working relative link from projects.html to ../day02/index.html
Any external link opens in a new tab with rel="noopener"

hints: Copy nothing from Day 2. Start with the shared header and nav on index.html, make it work, then build projects.html.
A relative path is relative to the file you are in. From day03/projects.html, your Day 2 page is one folder up: ../day02/index.html.

Good alt text describes what the image shows for someone who can't see it, e.g. alt="Me standing in front of my college library". Nest a <ul> inside an <li> or an <article>, not directly inside another <ul>.
proof: Commit with day03/index.html, day03/projects.html and your image.

explainBack.q: Take one relative link from your own pages. Explain how the browser works out which file to open.
lookFor: path resolved from the current file's folder
../ goes up one folder
cites their actual href

explainBack.q: Read out the alt text you wrote. Who uses it and when?
lookFor: screen reader users
shown if the image fails to load
search engines
describes the content not the word image

explainBack.q: You used header, nav, main and footer instead of divs. What does that change if the page looks exactly the same?
lookFor: meaning for screen readers and landmarks navigation
SEO / browser understands structure
easier to read code
looks don't change because they are block elements without default styling

lastHintExplanation: Relative paths are resolved from the folder of the current file, so ../ means 'go up one folder'. Alt text is read by screen readers and shown if the image fails to load. Semantic elements look like divs, but they tell browsers and assistive tech what each region is (landmarks), so users can jump straight to the nav or the main content.

predict.q: Your file is at day03/index.html and contains <a href="projects.html">. Which file opens?
options: Nothing, you need the full URL
predict.why: A relative path starts from the current file's folder, which is day03/.

predict.q: but me.jpg doesn't exist. What appears?
options: A broken-image icon and/or the alt text "Me at college"
The browser downloads a default image
predict.why: When the image can't load, the browser shows the alt text (often with a broken-image icon).

title: Forms and tables
goal: Build an accessible form and a correctly structured table.

concepts: <form action method>, what happens on submit
<label for> linked to <input id>; why every input needs a label
Input types: text, email, number, date, radio, checkbox; select, textarea
The name attribute: what gets sent to the server
Built-in validation: required, min, max, type=email
<table> with thead, tbody, th (scope), td, caption

build.task: In day04/index.html build a "Join the study group" form and your weekly study timetable. The form has name, email, year of study (select), preferred time (radio: morning/evening), topics (checkboxes: HTML, CSS, JS), a short message (textarea) and a submit button, using action="https://httpbin.org/post" method="post" so you can see what gets sent. The timetable is a table with a caption, days as column headers and time slots as row headers.
acceptance: Every control has a <label> linked with for/id (click the label: the input gets focus)
Every control has a name; radio buttons share one name
Email and name are required; empty submit is blocked by the browser
Submitting shows your data on httpbin.org under "form"
Table uses caption, thead, tbody, and th with scope="col" / scope="row"

hints: Build one field at a time and submit after each to see it appear on httpbin.
Radio buttons are one group when they share the same name. Each gets its own id and label, and its own value.
A row header looks like <th scope="row">9–10 AM</th> as the first cell of each body row; column headers live in <thead> with scope="col".
proof: Commit with day04/index.html. Paste the httpbin "form" output into the commit message body.

explainBack.q: In your httpbin result, which attribute of each input decided the key names you saw? Give one example from your form.
lookFor: name attribute becomes the key
value is what the user entered or the value attribute
example from their form

explainBack.q: Pick one label in your form. What does linking it with for/id do for users?
lookFor: clicking label focuses or checks the input
screen readers announce the label
bigger click target

explainBack.q: Why are your day names in th and not td? What does scope add?
lookFor: th marks header cells
scope tells whether header applies to column or row
screen readers read headers with each cell

lastHintExplanation: On submit, the browser sends each control's name with its value; controls without a name are not sent, and unchecked checkboxes send nothing. A label linked by for/id makes the text clickable and is what screen readers announce. th with scope marks header cells so assistive tech can say 'Monday, 9–10 AM: DSA' for each data cell.

title: CSS basics: selectors, cascade and the box model
goal: Style your Day 3 site with an external stylesheet and explain exactly why each rule wins.

concepts: Linking a stylesheet: <link rel="stylesheet" href>
Selectors: element, .class, #id, descendant, :hover
Cascade and specificity: which rule wins and why
Box model: content, padding, border, margin
box-sizing: border-box
Units: px, rem, %; colors and fonts
Using DevTools (F12 → Elements → Styles / Computed) to inspect rules

build.task: Copy your Day 3 site into day05/ and add css/style.css. Style it: a base font and colors on body, a header with padding and a bottom border, nav links styled with a :hover state, a centered main column (max-width with auto margins), and project articles as boxes with padding, border and margin. Add box-sizing: border-box for all elements. Include one deliberate specificity conflict and a comment explaining which rule wins.

starterFiles.name: day05/css/style.css

acceptance: No inline style attributes; all CSS in css/style.css
Uses element, class and id selectors at least once each, plus :hover
Main column is centered with max-width and margin auto
box-sizing: border-box applied to all elements
A comment in the CSS explains one specificity conflict and which rule wins

hints: Check the link works first: put body { background: yellow; } and refresh. If nothing changes, the href path is wrong.
To center a block: give it a max-width and margin: 0 auto. Use DevTools → Computed to see the box model numbers.
Specificity: id (1,0,0) beats class (0,1,0) beats element (0,0,1). Make a p with class="note" and style both p and .note with different colors; .note wins.

explainBack.q: Explain the specificity conflict you wrote in your CSS: which selectors compete, which wins, and why?
lookFor: specificity calculation id > class > element
later rule wins only when specificity is equal
cites their selectors

explainBack.q: On one of your project boxes, what is the difference between the padding and the margin you set? What would you see if you swapped them?
lookFor: padding is inside the border, background shows through
margin is outside the border, space between boxes
references their values

explainBack.q: What does box-sizing: border-box change about how your width or max-width is calculated?
lookFor: width includes padding and border
content-box adds padding and border on top of width
prevents overflow surprises

lastHintExplanation: When two rules target the same element, the one with higher specificity wins (ids beat classes, classes beat elements); only on a tie does the later rule win. Padding is space inside the border (the background fills it); margin is space outside, between elements. With border-box, the width you set includes padding and border, so boxes don't grow unexpectedly.

predict.why: A class selector (0,1,0) is more specific than an element selector (0,0,1).
An id selector beats a class selector regardless of order.

predict.q: A box has width: 200px; padding: 20px; border: 5px solid; and the default box-sizing. How wide is it on screen?
predict.why: content-box: 200 + 2×20 + 2×5 = 250px. With border-box it would be 200px.
